keyFindings.description: The deployment's own cluster namespace is written out in a shell command on a public branch: the departure record quotes the specification's `kubectl -n <namespace> get jobs,pods,svc`. The guidance this change ships is clean — it uses placeholders and reads the namespace from the projected token — and that care is undone one file away. `.github/scripts/check-private-names.sh` cannot see a namespace name, so the lint job's green is no evidence, and the tester's own private-name check covered the five non-handoff paths only (`test.json` proof 2). The fix at the head is the sentence without the command; whether the pushed commit that carries the blob must also be rewritten is the architect's call, since the branch is public.

The one step that demonstrates reaching the workload cannot run where the section says it runs. The block is introduced as "from a role container holding nothing but its checkout and that credential", and its payoff is `psql "postgres://…" -c 'select 1'`. The worker image ships no PostgreSQL client: `worker.Dockerfile:491` is the runtime stage's only apt line (ca-certificates chromium curl git jq openssh-client python3 socat util-linux wget), the toolchain capability row enumerates the image's tools without it, and `which psql` in this role container finds nothing. The section forbids the two ways out — no `exec` into the workload's pod, and installing in the pod is the withheld `operator-setup` row — so a role that follows it has a four-processor workload it cannot reach by any documented means. Demonstrate it with something the image has (`socat`, `python3`) or say that the client arrives the way the section already prescribes for checkout tools.

Nothing tells a role to name its workload for its issue, in a namespace every project's agents share under one identity — which the section itself states two paragraphs later. The example is `name: <workload>   # yours`, the Service selects `job-name: <workload>`, and the sequence ends `kubectl delete job <workload>`. Two roles that pick the same obvious name (`postgres`, `db`) collide: the second applies over the first's Job or is refused by its immutable fields, waits on the first's pod by label, queries the first's database, and its delete takes the first's running workload and Service with it. Every other object this runbook creates is scoped by issue (`issue-legion-<project>-<issue key lowercased>` at :730 and :1847), and the implementer's own live run used `infra71-doc`, a convention the document never states. One clause fixes it.

The gate's `no` branch is not what a role in a deployment that projects no credential sees. Every Legion pod sets `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, the image carries no kubeconfig and sets no `KUBECONFIG`, so `kubectl` has no in-cluster configuration to build and falls back to its default server. Measured here, in a pod that does have the credential, with the in-cluster environment removed: `couldn't get current server API group list: Get "http://localhost:8080/api?timeout=32s": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connect: connection refused` and then `Warning: the server doesn't have a resource type 'jobs'` — at exit status 0, so a role could read it as success. Say that no credential means the command cannot reach a cluster at all, and that this is as conclusive as `no`.

The admission list's promise is untrue of its last bullet. The list is introduced with "a workload that breaks one is refused at submission with a message naming the rule it broke, so nothing here has to be taken on trust", and the reachability-label bullet is not that kind of rule: by its own next sentence an unlabelled workload is admitted, started, charged against the shared quota and reachable by nothing. Neither the implementer's eight breakages nor the tester's nineteen covers a missing label, because there is no refusal to measure. The one mistake with no refusal is the one the reader is told not to guard against; move it to the Service paragraph or qualify the promise.

The section never says where to write `workload.yaml` and `service.yaml`, and a role's working directory is a jj/git checkout of this public repository, so a manifest carrying the password it just chose is snapshotted into the working-copy commit and can reach the branch — the very acceptance this branch records (`jj diff --name-only` equal to the issue's file list) is what a stray manifest breaks. One clause putting both files outside the checkout fixes it, and keeps the password out of `psql`'s argv at :2576 as well.

The architect's own conditional, folded in since the round requests changes anyway: the sequence's last command is refused `Forbidden` on services until the declarations are applied, after the clean-up has already succeeded. The section says above that this is the pre-apply state, so nothing is wrong, but a clause on that line keeps a role from reading the refusal as its own mistake.

verified: CI at code head 75e45efd: 25 check runs, none unsuccessful at the read, the required lint, typecheck, test and pr-title all success; compare 75e45efd...437b780e is .legion/ only.
The branch is this issue's work alone: nine paths, the install step and the pinned-tool guard both off it, and no file of either half remains — only the handoff ledger mentions them, as history.

The narrowed `network` row is consistent at capabilities.go:99, the golden fixture, worker.Dockerfile's comment and both other quotations in docs/kubernetes.md; Site and Ruling are unchanged, so every test holding withheld rows still holds.
No name of the deployment's cluster in the added lines of the nine paths, in any commit message of this generation, in the PR title or in its body — the one exception is the blocking finding above.
Three threads of the superseded scope answered: two are moot with the install step, and the guard's two open findings are named for dispatch://INFRA-199 rather than left to die with the file.
